methodological_rigor.justification: The study triangulates the miR-21/SASH1 link using TCGA miRNA-seq comparisons (347 tumors vs 50 adjacent tissues), a small paired human tissue set (8 HBV-HCC tumors with adjacent non-tumor), cell-line perturbations (inhibitor/mimic, siSASH1), and an orthotopic HepG2.2.15 mouse model with four treatment arms. Key design limitations are the very small clinical cohort, use of essentially one HBV-integrated HCC line for most functional work, and incomplete reporting of in vivo experimental details (e.g., the number of mice per group, blinding/allocation concealment, and any sample-size justification are not stated). Statistical methods are standard but basic (t-tests/ANOVA with Bonferroni; mean ± SEM; 'at least three independent experiments') and do not describe handling of missing data or any pre-specified analysis plan.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is primarily preclinical/mechanistic work (cell lines and an orthotopic mouse xenograft) with supportive expression analyses in TCGA and a small set of human HBV-HCC tissues, so the Oxford level of evidence is 5. The clinical question is relevant (sorafenib resistance in HBV-associated HCC) and the intervention concept is actionable in principle (miR-21 inhibition combined with sorafenib), but efficacy is only demonstrated in models without patient outcome data. Endpoints are largely surrogate/biologic (proliferation, apoptosis signaling, tumor suppression in mice) rather than direct clinical endpoints.

reporting_quality.justification: Given the in vivo orthotopic mouse component, ARRIVE is the closest fit; the manuscript reports species/strain/age/sex, tumor implantation approach, dosing schedules, and humane endpoints, but omits several checklist-critical details such as per-group sample sizes, blinding, and any randomization method beyond stating mice were 'randomly divided'. Methods for assays and statistical testing are described, yet reporting is uneven (e.g., reliance on figure-referenced outcomes with limited tabulated detail in the normalized text). Data/code sharing is not described beyond referring to supplementary tables for sequences/antibodies/primers, so reproducibility rests mainly on narrative methods without accessible raw data or analysis code.

novelty_literature.justification: miR-21 as an oncogenic miRNA and sorafenib resistance in HCC are well-trodden areas, making the overall concept incremental. The more specific contribution is positioning SASH1 as a direct miR-21 target in an HBV/HBx-linked resistance context and showing combination benefit with sorafenib in an orthotopic HBV-HCC model. The novelty is therefore a meaningful mechanistic extension rather than a first-in-class therapeutic or paradigm change.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is organized in a conventional IMRaD structure with clearly labeled methods subsections (e.g., luciferase assay, orthotopic model, statistical analysis) and results presented as stepwise mechanistic claims. The abstract is largely self-contained and aligns with the stated experiments (TCGA/tissue expression, target validation, in vitro sensitization, and in vivo combination effect). Some claims would benefit from more explicit numeric detail in the text (e.g., in vivo group sizes and effect magnitudes), but overall clarity is good for a preclinical translational paper.

key_strengths: Multi-layer evidence linking miR-21 to SASH1 downregulation (bioinformatic prediction plus luciferase 3′-UTR assays and inhibitor/mimic perturbations).
Includes both human data context (TCGA comparisons and an 8-patient HBV-HCC tissue set) and in vivo testing (orthotopic HepG2.2.15 model with sorafenib plus miR-21 inhibitor).
Mechanistic framing connects HBV/HBx-associated signaling (PI3K/AKT/mTOR) to drug response, yielding a coherent translational hypothesis.
key_concerns: Limited clinical evidence: the human cohort is very small and there are no patient-level response/outcome data to support therapeutic claims.
In vivo rigor is under-reported (no per-arm mouse n, no blinding details, and no sample-size/power justification), weakening confidence in effect estimates.
Generalizability is constrained by reliance on a narrow set of models (notably HepG2.2.15 for HBV-integrated context) and short-term surrogate endpoints.
Reproducibility posture is weak with no explicit raw data or code availability statement in the manuscript text.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The work is a solid preclinical mechanistic extension with an in vivo combination signal, but limited clinical validation and incomplete reporting of key in vivo design elements keep it below top-tier translational journals and warrant major revisions.
